Text | Er Mu

Editing | Er Mu, Fanyu Meng

At some point, desert holidays became all the rage, in China and abroad alike:

camel rides under the blazing sun by day,

stargazing flat on your back by night.

What could be more blissful!

But besides these two standard activities, did you know that some deserts also treat you to a low growling and booming from the sand itself?

“Shapotou lies on a jutting desert terrace on the southern edge of the Tengger Desert, where it meets the Yellow River. On the north side of the terrace rises a sand dune about one hundred meters high. When you slide down from its crest, a humming boom rises from deep within the earth, now like the waves of the sea, now like the long peal of a golden bell. Add the babbling of the hidden streams that flow from the foot of the dune into the Yellow River, and the famous ‘Singing Bell of the Sand Slope’ becomes all the more of a spectacle.”

The passage above comes from a description of the booming sand at Shapotou in Ningxia, one of China’s best-known desert attractions.

People have in fact been noticing and recording the booming of deserts for a thousand years. As early as 1295, Marco Polo described this extraordinary sound in his famous Travels, along with the fear it inspired:

“The desert spirits can do amazing and incredible things. Even in the daytime their voices can sometimes be heard, or there is a clash of arms, a roll of drums or the sound of different musical instruments. For these reasons, travelers go in large numbers and stay close to one another.”

The booming heard in deserts is generally concentrated between 50 and 300 Hz. It carries a long way, up to 10 km, and can last a long time: the longest recorded boom went on for 15 minutes. Some say it sounds like drums, some like thunder, and others like a helicopter skimming low overhead.

Have a listen below (best with loudspeakers or over-ear headphones):

So why do deserts boom like this? People living near Shapotou put it down to a beautiful legend, while Marco Polo blamed evil spirits or goblins.

Marco Polo: Evil inside!!!

As upstanding 21st-century “big eaters” (a tongue-in-cheek Chinese buzzword for people who live for their next meal), we naturally put our faith in science.

Sadly, this time science has not yet given us a perfect explanation either: the mechanism behind the booming of dunes is still debated. What we do know is that the boom is caused by avalanches on the dune, as sand flows down from the crest.

But how does sand flowing down a dune produce a low-frequency boom? Some have proposed a friction theory: the sound comes from grains rubbing against each other and from air being squeezed in the gaps between them. Others have put forward a shear theory: when the dune avalanches, nonlinear oscillations in the shear layer as it disperses stress cause the boom. Still others think the boom comes from a resonant cavity formed by dry and damp layers near the dune surface, and so on. None of these theories is complete, none has convinced the other camps, and the scientific argument will go on.

Although the mechanism is not understood, researchers have still compiled some of the conditions a dune needs in order to boom, because not every dune booms when it avalanches.

The sand in booming dunes differs from ordinary dune sand in two main ways: the grains have smoother surfaces and greater resistance to shear. Other factors that favor booming are grains of as uniform a size as possible, with rounded surfaces and no sharp edges.

As for what the sand is made of, almost all booming dunes consist of quartz sand. The one exception is the back-beach booming dune on Niihau Island in Hawaii, the only booming dune found so far that is not made of quartz: its sand consists mainly of calcium carbonate from seashells. The sand also needs to be as dry as possible, because in damp sand the water forms a lubricating film on the grains that reduces their resistance to shear.

At this point, some of you may be thinking that scientists really are a stubborn and rather pointless bunch. They travel day and night, covered in dust, out to the wilderness, not to search for lost ancient cities or buried treasure but to risk their necks working out where a sound comes from. Very odd. And even once they have worked it out, what use is it?

How a desert trip is supposed to look

Here is what they get up to in the desert. Notice how they trigger sand avalanches by hand to make the dune boom.

Many (innovative) areas of science really do follow researchers’ own “pointless” interests, and the results may seem to have no use. But that uselessness is often only true at the time of the research and does not last into the future. Or it may hold only within one field, while in another field the same work opens up a whole new vista.

Dr Nathalie Vriend, a Royal Society Dorothy Hodgkin Research Fellow in the Department of Applied Mathematics and Theoretical Physics at the University of Cambridge, has been working on the strange sound that troubled Marco Polo ever since her PhD project at Caltech, and her research is still connected with it today. She has said that understanding how booming dunes produce their sound could be a great help to both the pharmaceutical industry and oil and gas exploration.

The sand avalanches that cause the booming belong to the field of granular flow, and making medicines involves the flow and mixing of granules of several ingredients. In oil and gas exploration in the desert, a sound source is usually placed at one spot and sensors at several others to pick up its signal; analyzing the received signals reveals what lies hidden underground. Understanding how the booming is generated and how it propagates through the desert would help make such surveys more accurate.

Useful as all that is, she still put it with Zen-like calm:

“What I love about my research, whether it’s looking at silos or avalanches, is that you can observe it, see it, feel it, touch it.”
